items.title: Do not go gentle into that good night
items.author: Dylan Thomas
items.standfirst: A year spent looking, then a shelf of everything worth keeping, and now the poem that says what the looking was for. It is the shortest thing on this page: nineteen lines, one instruction, repeated until it stops being advice.
items.sourceLabel: Read the poem at Poetry Foundation ↗
items.note: Kept here because the light was never the reward. Catching it, and not letting go, was the whole instruction.

Do not go gentle into that good night.
Rage, rage against the dying of the light.
stanzas: Do not go gentle into that good night,
Old age should burn and rave at close of day;
Rage, rage against the dying of the light.
Though wise men at their end know dark is right,
Because their words had forked no lightning they
Do not go gentle into that good night.
Good men, the last wave by, crying how bright
Their frail deeds might have danced in a green bay,
Rage, rage against the dying of the light.
Wild men who caught and sang the sun in flight,
And learn, too late, they grieved it on its way,
Do not go gentle into that good night.
Grave men, near death, who see with blinding sight
Blind eyes could blaze like meteors and be gay,
Rage, rage against the dying of the light.
And you, my father, there on the sad height,
Curse, bless, me now with your fierce tears, I pray.
Do not go gentle into that good night.
Rage, rage against the dying of the light.

items.title: When You Are Old
items.author: William Butler Yeats
items.standfirst: An old age imagined beside the fire: a book opened, a remembered face, and the rare love that saw beyond beauty.
items.sourceLabel: Read the poem at Poetry Foundation ↗
items.note: A quiet invitation to remember the one who loved the pilgrim soul beneath the passing years.
stanzas: When you are old and grey and full of sleep,
And nodding by the fire, take down this book,
And slowly read, and dream of the soft look
Your eyes had once, and of their shadows deep;
How many loved your moments of glad grace,
And loved your beauty with love false or true,
But one man loved the pilgrim soul in you,
And loved the sorrows of your changing face;
And bending down beside the glowing bars,
Murmur, a little sadly, how Love fled
And paced upon the mountains overhead
And hid his face amid a crowd of stars.

items.title: Nobody knows this little Rose
items.author: Emily Dickinson
items.standfirst: A small rose carried from the ways and offered in secret, noticed only by the creatures that might have missed it.
items.note: The rose passes briefly through a world of roads, wings, weather and attention.
stanzas: Nobody knows this little Rose –
It might a pilgrim be
Did I not take it from the ways
And lift it up to thee.
Only a Bee will miss it –
Only a Butterfly,
Hastening from far journey –
On it′s breast to lie –
Only a Bird will wonder –
Only a Breeze will sigh –
Ah Little Rose – how easy
For such as thee to die!
